claim: A 5-year study found a civil engineering technology capstone design course has curricular merit but fails as an effective outcomes-assessment tool.
stance_target: using a single capstone/major project course to measure program-level outcome attainment (as NBA/ABET-style frameworks do)
scope_conditions: Southern Polytechnic State University, civil engineering technology, 5-year longitudinal study
quoted_support: The study clearly demonstrated that the course has merit in the curriculum but fails as an outcomes assessment tool.

claim: The primary obstacle to using capstone projects for outcomes assessment is quantification: findings remain anecdotal because many relevant outcomes are intangible and not readily measurable.
stance_target: capstone/major projects are structurally weak instruments for rigorous, comparable outcome measurement
scope_conditions: Southern Polytechnic State University capstone assessment study
quoted_support: It is shown that the primary difficulty faced when attempting to use a capstone design course as an assessment tool lies with the quantification of findings.

claim: Outcomes assessment is frequently and incorrectly conflated with faculty evaluation by both faculty and administrators, undermining its intended curricular-improvement purpose.
stance_target: institutional dynamics around project-based outcome assessment
quoted_support: the words 'outcomes assessment' are often interpreted as 'faculty evaluation' regardless of what administrators or others may say.

claim: An effective outcomes-assessment tool must be easy to administer, or institutions become reluctant to run it and instead perform assessment only to satisfy accreditation checkboxes.
stance_target: design requirements for a workable outcomes-assessment mechanism
quoted_support: an effective outcomes assessment tool must be easy to administer. If great difficulty is encountered gathering and analyzing data two mindsets develop... It is suggested that many schools conduct assessment activities because of accreditation requirements not because they think the activities will lead to a better curriculum.
